article_text:
Linda Duncombe , a longtime banking executive who spent the last past years as an independent film producer, died on Sunday of complications from a stroke. She was 55.

An infectiously friendly face at industry events, Duncombe — who was diagnosed with Stage 2 lung cancer days before she died — served for five years as chief marketing officer at City National Bank. She helped direct more than $12 million in investments tied to organizations such as Habitat for Humanity, Broadway Cares, SAG-AFTRA and the Grammy Museum.

Duncombe’s last public appearance was at the Motion Picture & Television Fund’s “The Evening Before” the Primetime Emmy Awards on Sept. 13, where she reunited with friends and rubbed shoulders with some of Hollywood’s biggest stars.

Popular on Variety

Born on Feb. 10, 1971 in Australia, where she spent the early years of her life, Duncombe enrolled in Harvard Business School in 2008. She officially moved to the United States in 2015, first living in New York and then in an apartment near the beach in Santa Monica. She produced two movies: the family adventure “The Queen’s Jewels” and suspense thriller “Killing Time.” Both films are planning a global release in 2027, and Duncombe was intricately involved in all elements of production from financing to publicity.

“Linda was a source of light, always smiling, laughing, gossiping — which, she’d say to her friends, ‘is never gossip between us, love’ — and someone who adored Hollywood with all her heart,” says Variety’s co-president and co-editor-in-chief Ramin Setoodeh, a close friend. “Growing up as a young girl in Australia, she dreamed of finding her way in the film industry. In the last few years, she finally realized her calling as a producer, which made her beam even more. This is a devastating loss, and I will miss Linda so much.”

Duncombe began her decades-long banking career at Citibank in Australia in 2010 as marketing director of digital and customer experience and rose to managing director, head of growth and chief marketing officer. Five years later, she transferred to New York as a founding member of the company’s subsidiary, Citi Fintech.

She joined City National Bank in Los Angeles in early 2019, establishing business, sponsorship and community relations with organizations like SAG-AFTRA Foundation, the Recording Academy, the Motion Picture Television Fund and Tribeca Festival. During the pandemic, she led efforts at City National Bank to deliver more than $1.8 billion in Paycheck Protection Program loans to support the entertainment industry.

At City National Bank, she quickly became friends with Variety staffers while working to keep the magazine’s annual “Business of Broadway Breakfast” afloat during COVID. Over the years, the event has attracted theater mainstays from Lin-Manuel Miranda to Rachel Zegler.

“Linda was initially my client but quickly became my very good friend, always including me in her gatherings,” says Variety publisher and co-president Dea Lawrence. “A true warrior woman who understood the importance of shared experiences and letting go with that unforgettable, infectious laugh. She was fiercely loyal, endlessly generous, and embraced life with so much passion and heart. It is hard to fathom that her brilliant light has gone out.”

Duncombe’s friends remember her sunny spirit, boisterous laughter, unbridled optimism and passion for new experiences. She took pride in mentoring younger generations and was deeply loyal to those in her orbit. Duncombe’s inner circle included her producing partner and best friend Josh Friedman, who was always by her side at industry events.

“Losing Linda is going to change the lives of so many people,” says Friedman, whom Duncombe affectionately called her little brother. “She made life look really easy in managing many things but remaining the most humble, kind and generous person. The emojis next to her name in my phone were a princess, heart and unicorn. She was a unicorn in this life for a lot of people.”

Added Bob Beitcher, MPTF’s president and CEO, “Linda was a gift to everyone who knew her. She was vital, fun, whip-smart, caring and compassionate, and always, always there to lend a hand and lift you up. As a friend and advisor, she is irreplaceable, and her passing dims the light for me and for MPTF.”

Duncombe was recognized on Variety’s “Most Powerful Women in Hollywood” list and was honored by the Australian Governor General with the Order of Australia Medal. She sat on the boards of several groups including the SAG-AFTRA Foundation, Grammy Museum, Habitat for Humanity Greater L.A. and the Australian Wildlife Conservancy.

After leaving Australia, Duncombe was proud of the success she’d achieved in the decade in which she lived in the United States.

“As a 9-year-old, I told my parents I wanted to live in New York when I grew up. My parents did not hesitate in their support of a shy, young girl’s big dreams,” she told the magazine Beauty Is in 2025 . “We lived in government housing and while we had no money, our family and home was rich in love, support and laughter.”

As a child, she was inspired by the “Wonder Woman” television series starring Lynda Carter, and her parents taught her that treating people with kindness and respect would make her unstoppable. “Now I am a woman who has worked hard,” she said. “I try my very best to share my learnings, experiences, and networks to help people go after their dreams and live their best life.”

She is survived by her mother, Doreen Thompson, and nieces and nephews Shannen, Damien and Jarred.

Introduction

Returning to his childhood home deep in Colorado’s mountains, Mike is drawn back into the quiet rituals of family life, as if time had stood still. But when his mother suddenly disappears in the season’s first snowstorm, the familiar order begins to unravel, leaving Mike to negotiate new dynamics with his father as he searches for his own sense of self and belonging. Adapting Brooklyn novelist Colm Tóibín’s short story, Haigh’s (45 Years, All of Us Strangers) intimate drama delicately uncovers hidden fractures within the family, revealing unspoken truths.

Hyun Jin Cho

Content advice

Contains scenes of animal slaughter.

How to book

Tickets start from £10 for all screenings and events in London, with concessions available for many screenings. Booking information and ticket prices .

For non-Members we charge £1 per ticket for online and phone bookings, up to £3 per transaction. There’s no booking fee if you buy tickets at the box office.

If you’re aged 16 to 25, sign up for free to BFI 25 and Under for a chance to get £6 tickets (without booking fees) to all screenings and events, subject to availability.

Missed out?

More tickets may become available for these screenings before and during the festival. Find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Our programmers recommend...

The Man I Love

Ira Sachs cements his position as one of the great chroniclers of New York life with this tender, earthy portrait of the city’s gay scene in the 1980s.

Frank and Percy

Roger Allam and Ian McKellen excel as the titular characters in this adaptation of the West End hit, about finding connection beyond your sixties.

The Idiot(s)

article_text:
New York’s Massey Klein Gallery will close its doors after nine years, saying that after initial success, the numbers no longer add up to pay for its showroom on the Lower East Side and support the dealers’ family and the gallery’s artists.

Husband-and-wife team Garrett Klein and Ryan Massey felt called by their Christian faith to open the gallery, and say they’ll continue on with nomadic projects. They announced the closure in a Saturday Instagram post. The gallery’s current show, of Kate McQuillen, is extended through November 20.

The gallery has participated in prominent fairs including the Armory Show and NADA in New York, Untitled in Miami, and the Dallas Art Fair. At NADA New York in 2025, ARTnews ’s Harrison Jacobs noted its display as one of the fair’s best .

“Our relationship with God has informed what we want the gallery to feel like,” said Klein in a phone interview. “We’re all accustomed to feeling uninvited at galleries. We wanted to create a place of warmth.”

“Previously, sales were up steadily, and we were hitting benchmarks each year,” said Klein. “But four years ago, we started to go into decline. We were hoping that by this point we would start to see a leveling out. We’ve always been sensitive to the numbers. We never had a large nest egg to start a gallery. We have to sell the work. We’re religious, and it seemed like we were pushed into this place where we could take that leap of faith but with the numbers declining so much we’ve had to figure out other jobs to do.”

The couple opened with just enough to secure a lease and cover a month’s rent, says their farewell announcement. Both the founders had worked at other New York galleries, Klein principally with Bertrand Delacroix and Massey at Mulherin and Pollard. “We were blessed with some amazing sales right out of the gate,” said Klein. But the gallery sells works by emerging artists in the range of $3,000 to $20,000, and has to sell $30,000 to $40,000 a month to comfortably cover expenses, including rent, which comes in at a little under $10,000 a month for the 1,000-square-foot gallery.

Massey Klein has been a small operation all along, and currently represents just six artists—Chrissy Angliker, Lydia Baker, Bethany Czarnecki, Jude Greibel, and Laura Sallade, along with McQuillen. Klein says they’ve done their best to keep the artists abreast of the challenges so that this news wouldn’t be a shock.

Many galleries have closed in recent months in a challenging market, some of them putting out farewell statements that blamed the art market system, some closing amid legal battles, some simply saying business had fallen off a cliff and prices for services like storage and shipping have implacably risen. Massey Klein’s signoff may be the only one that discusses a prayer practice that was intertwined with the gallery. Klein said he would usually start his day with a brief mediation and prayer, and that they had sometimes invited others from their Christian church community to prayer events.

View this post on Instagram

As for the future, the dealers hope to continue showing at some of the art fairs they’ve previously participated in. They will still participate next year in New York’s Split Level art fair, its third edition, and will continue to organize art displays with Groupe NYC, a collective of clothing designers with a showroom on the Bowery nearby.

L.A.’s historic Bruin Theatre met its ambitious fall reopening target on Friday, October 23, but its return is already facing a challenge from the companies behind its first attraction. Laika and Fathom Entertainment say they have taken legal action to stop the Bruin from showing “ Wildwood .”

The film was previously advertised as a week-long run at the newly reopened Westwood venue. But in a joint statement provided exclusively to IndieWire, the animation studio and its theatrical distribution partner said concerns about operator Rui Pereira ‘s history of controversial comments and behavior prompted them to seek an end to screenings.

“When Laika became aware of the Bruin engagement, we immediately raised concerns with Fathom Entertainment, our theatrical distribution partner. Laika and Fathom commenced legal action to end the film’s screenings at the theatre,” the companies said in an email.

“We have not yet received confirmation that the screenings have stopped. We are continuing to explore our options, as the concerns regarding the theatre operator are incompatible with the values of our two companies.” IndieWire independently confirmed that “Wildwood” screenings had continued at the Bruin through at least Sunday afternoon, October 25, and as of publication, the theater’s website still advertised daily screenings at 1:30 p.m., 4 p.m., 7 p.m., and 9:30 p.m.

Laika and Fathom Entertainment did not specify what kind of legal action they had taken to stop showings of their film. On a phone call with IndieWire, Pereira asked how we had obtained a cease-and-desist letter. IndieWire had neither received nor reviewed such a letter and told Pereira we had communicated directly with the companies. He continued, “You guys are assholes. Everything you have written is false.”

The dispute introduces an immediate programming problem for Pereira’s revived movie palace, which reopened with “Wildwood” after sitting dark since Regency Theatres departed the space in July 2024 . It also follows months of scrutiny involving Pereira, whose rocky history operating Toronto’s Kingsway Theatre became the subject of an IndieWire investigation on September 3.

IndieWire’s earlier reporting examined allegations of assault, nonpayment, racial discrimination, online harassment, and unauthorized film exhibition . The reporting drew on interviews with more than 25 sources in the U.S. and Canada, as well as court records, digital correspondence, social media posts, and years of advertised Kingsway screenings some rights holders say they did not authorize. Pereira has broadly disputed those allegations and characterized the ongoing scrutiny of his businesses as an effort to undermine his work as an exhibitor.

“There are no controversies and any attempt to generate them is dishonest and disingenuous,” Pereira said then. “The Bruin Theater is a gift, not only to Los Angeles, but the world — a cultural heritage site that unites generations of movie goers in the experience of cinema.”

Several journalists have described being targeted by Pereira after publishing critical coverage or omitting the Kingsway from their reporting. Speaking with IndieWire on the phone and in a subsequent email on October 26, Pereira referred to IndieWire staff as “presstitutes” and accused the publication of getting paid to write about him negatively.

Two volunteers left the Bruin restoration project in August after posts attributed to the Kingsway account circulated among Los Angeles moviegoers. Screenshots reviewed by IndieWire included racist and antisemitic remarks, as well as exchanges targeting individual patrons. Sources also described threats and a pattern of prolonged retaliation, alleging that Pereira continued targeting some critics online for months or years after their initial disputes.

When asked by The Hollywood Reporter in an August 23 report about some specific Kingsway posts — including one telling a target to “Go back to Poland” and another describing a swastika painted on a Jewish family’s home as “the proper symbol for zionazis” — Pereira acknowledged that the comments were “offensive” and said he “must take responsibility.”

The current dispute over “Wildwood” also follows separate questions about the Kingsway’s programming. IndieWire previously identified 55 advertised screenings of 17 films that three rights holders said they had not authorized at Pereira’s Toronto theater. Those findings came from a limited sample and did not establish that all or even most Kingsway screenings were unlicensed. “There are no issues with film licensing or any disputes,” Pereira said previously.

Notably, Laika and Fathom’s statement does not suggest that the Bruin’s “Wildwood” booking was unauthorized from the outset. Rather, the companies say they sought to end the Bruin screenings over specific concerns about Pereira as operator. “Wildwood” opened in nearly 3,000 theaters nationwide , and a booking on that scale is hardly an endorsement of every exhibitor.

Still, independent theaters often build their identities around the taste and reputations of the people running them. At a beloved landmark like the Bruin, affection for an old movie palace can translate into intense trust in whoever promises to save it. For now, the location has achieved the reopening its new operator promised. Whether it can continue showing the film that brought audiences back is in dispute.

article_text:
A work of deep personal reckoning, Yi-Shan Lo’s debut documentary feature opens with closeups of the film-maker’s own footsteps as she trudges through a snowbound landscape. Her jagged movement mirrors the rugged trajectory of the film itself, which grapples with a harrowing tragedy. In 2017, Lo was about to join her best friends Chun and Yueh on their hiking trip across Nepal when she came down with a sudden illness; she decided to stay behind while the other two carried on. Disaster struck: the pair went missing during a heavy snowstorm and were not found for more than 40 days. Yueh survived, but Chun died from lack of food coupled with hypothermia.

Struggling to make sense of these events, Lo painstakingly retraces the days leading up to and during her friends’ disappearance. She pores over old text messages, Chun’s diaries and footage captured by the Nepali rescue team. These materials shed some light on the ordeal, as well as the pair’s backgrounds. Diving into her personal archive, Lo recalls her burgeoning friendship with Chun at their Catholic girls’ school, where the latter defiantly resisted the institution’s rigid dress codes. Considering Chun’s efforts to express his non-conforming identity and his use of male pronouns, it is even more devastating that he was repeatedly misgendered in death by various news reports.

Revelatory as they might be, these artefacts appear insubstantial next to the weight of grief. In the second half of the film, Lo physically returns to the trail of the fateful trek. As digital screens and paper scraps give way to the vistas of babbling brooks and verdant hills, film-making emerges as a cathartic gesture of remembrance. Through Lo’s lens, the cave where Chun and Yueh took shelter ceases only to be a site of trauma, but a shrine to the memories of their love.

article_text:
Hello Sunshine , which was recently re-acquired by co-founder Reese Witherspoon alongside France-based Mediawan , is laying off half of its staff.

The company produces film and TV titles along with maintaining a Witherspoon-branded book club. It is letting go of about 30 workers, a source familiar with the cutbacks told Deadline, was not unexpected and is part of an effort to refocus Hello Sunshine on its core strategic areas. Remaining employees are concentrating primarily on film, TV and the book club, along with related social and digital marketing as well as partnerships.

The Mediawan-Witherspoon acquisition earlier this month from Candle Media drew considerable attention in the industry given the steep drop in valuation over the past couple of years. The initial Candle deal valued Hello Sunshine at $900 million. While the recent transaction price was not disclosed, knowledgeable sources told Deadline that Candle, backed by private equity giant Blackstone, likely lost hundreds of millions of dollars on the deal.

A rep from Hello Sunshine declined to comment on the staff cuts when reached by Deadline.

Watch on Deadline

Private equity had previously been flowing into the entertainment business, with firms enticed by low interest rates and a seemingly bottomless appetite from Netflix and rival streamers. When the streaming platforms curtailed their spending on programming, many suppliers suffered, and a turbulent economy marked by rising rates and fuel costs did not help.

Mediawan’s properties also include Brad Pitt’s Plan B along with the Chernin Group. The company has “built a global, independent studio by putting creators first,” Witherspoon said in a statement earlier this month. “That has always been my vision for Hello Sunshine.”

Launched in 2016 with backing from Peter Chernin and Jesse Jacobs through The Chernin Group, Hello Sunshine has gone on to rack up a number of premium film and TV credits. Among them are Big Little Lies , The Morning Show , Where the Crawdads Sing , Little Fires Everywhere , Daisy Jones & The Six , From Scratc h and The Last Thing He Told Me .

Hello Sunshine co-founder Seth Rodsky has joined the company’s board alongside Witherspoon and representatives from Mediawan.

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE : Space 11 Corp. and SK Films are behind Return to the Moon: The Story of Artemis II , a new space film with Duncan Copp and Christopher Riley directing.

The producers are targeting a PLF rollout for the film, which they say will combine NASA’s real Artemis II mission imagery with the voices of the four astronauts who lived it. Worldwide theatrical release is targeted for summer 2027.

The synopsis reads: “Between April 1 and 11, 2026, the crew of the spacecraft Integrity traveled 695,081 miles and reached 252,756 miles from Earth, setting a new record for human spaceflight. The film follows the mission from the launch pad to splashdown in the Pacific.”

Space 11 says it is collaborating with NASA under a Space Act Agreement to shoot giant-screen interviews with the Artemis II crew: Commander Reid Wiseman, Pilot Victor Glover, Mission Specialist Christina Koch and Mission Specialist Jeremy Hansen of the Canadian Space Agency.

Watch on Deadline

The narrative will be interwoven by the four astronauts in their own words and NASA’s high-resolution photography and footage, reformatted for giant screens. A 45 minute version and a shorter format are being planned to go out via SK’s network of giant-screen and specialty theaters, including IMAX theaters, museums, science-centers, and other institutional venues. The film will also be offered to school groups.

Duncan Copp and Christopher Riley have both worked with NASA’s astronauts, engineers and scientists, past and present. Copp and Riley produced Ron Howard-presented In the Shadow of the Moon , winner of the World Cinema Documentary Audience Award at Sundance. Riley, a two-time BAFTA nominee, has worked with the Artemis II crew before, on hit immersive experience The Moonwalkers: A Journey with Tom Hanks , which he co-wrote with Hanks.

The film is produced by Andrea Iervolino ( Ferrari ), founder of Space 11. Producer Nicola Allieta will also participate in this production.

SK, the natural history and science content specialist, most recently released Ocean Dreams , narrated by Shailene Woodley.

Andrea Iervolino, Founder of Space 11, stated: “Artemis II belongs to everyone who looked up at the Moon in April. We are honored to tell this story in collaboration with NASA and alongside the four astronauts who took us there. Our responsibility is to make a film that everyone behind this mission, from the teams at NASA and the Canadian Space Agency to the families who waited at home, will watch with pride. With Duncan Copp and Christopher Riley, who know this crew and this history as few filmmakers do, and with SK Films, we will share that journey with audiences around the world.”

Bert Ulrich, Executive Vice President of Production at Space 11 and former NASA Film and Television Liaison, added: “In more than two decades at NASA, I learned that nothing moves people like real imagery and the voices of those who were actually there. This film is built on both: NASA’s own photography and footage, and the Artemis II crew recounting the flight themselves. On a giant screen, it is as close as most of us will ever come to flying aboard Integrity. If it inspires young people to reach for a seat on a future mission, it will have done what the best space documentaries have always done.”

“NASA’s Artemis II Mission is the perfect subject for giant screen cinema: it invites audiences to experience a historic accomplishment, with the extraordinarily personal perspective of its astronauts, on a scale unparalleled by any other cinematic experience” said Wendy MacKeigan, CEO of SK Films. “We are excited to be working with Space 11 and the brilliant creative team to bring this film to audiences around the world.”

article_text:
Turns out that it’s tough to shoot in a whale’s stomach.

“ Whalefall ” director Brian Duffield is gleefully outlining some of the biggest hurdles while shooting his new movie. The premise for the film, in theaters now via 20th Century Studios, is simple: A young diver named Jay ( Austin Abrams ) is accidentally swallowed by a whale, ends up in its stomach and must escape before his tank of oxygen runs out. It’s a lean idea, but required an innovative and energetic leader like Duffield to get the claustrophobic shots done on practical sets.

“It’s such a small space and essentially a 360-degree set,” he says. “There’s a couple portals you can kind of shove a camera through, but it’s also somewhat full of water. All the lighting of the coil is inside the set. Basically everything that you would have on a normal movie set, we’re putting inside of a very small space. It’s also on a gimbal that’s rocking and rolling. So you take your normal film set footprint and then you put it into a bag. And then you also put Austin Abrams into the bag, and then sometimes other animals. If Austin’s wrong an inch, it doesn’t really work. Everyone’s cramped in this little doorway. But he can’t hear us, because the rubber is so thick inside.”

Popular on Variety

Duffield smiles at the outrageous setup.

“I was talking to a director,” he says. “He had a question and I sent him pictures of the set. And he was just like, ‘You’ve got to be joking.’ From when the whale is chewing Austin, it’s just a bunch of big, burly men jumping on the set and crushing down on him. And he’s in there, screaming and drowning with a real oxygen tank. I’m looking at this little monitor and if he needs help, it’s going to sound the exact same. Every time you call cut, you’re just hoping that the screaming stops. We had the studio come to set and watch this thing. From the outside it just looked so silly. I remember Disney safety reps would come and just be watching it, saying, ‘I genuinely don’t know if this is safe.’ But we worked hard, really hard to make sure Austin was safe.”

Everyone made it out of the shoot unharmed, but the finished product is filled with harrowing set-pieces that are sure to push audiences to the brink. Duffield understood the vision early on, as he reached out to novelist Daniel Kraus on social media when he first heard the premise of the novel of the same name, before it was even published. He read an advance copy of the 2023 book, and was quickly swept away with the cinematic promise it held. Duffield ended up co-writing the “Whalefall” script with Kraus.

“You get the initial ‘boy inside a whale’ story, which definitely tickled all the genre parts of my brain,” Duffield says. “The idea of making a movie that had never been made before is always really appealing to me. It’s instantly clear how challenging that was, and I was really looking for a challenge. I was hungry to just keep pushing myself and the crew that I had consistently been working with. I think we just had the appetite at the time to take a big swing.”

Duffield is no stranger to ambitious projects. He began his Hollywood career as a writer with a disparate group of scripts, including a big-budget sequel (2015’s “The Divergent Series: Insurgent”), a Western (2015’s “Jane Got a Gun”), a slasher (2017’s “The Babysitter”) and a sci-fi action movie (2020’s “Underwater”). He transitioned into an idiosyncratic directing career with 2020’s “Spontaneous” (logline: a romance is shaded by the fact that people start spontaneously combusting) and 2023’s “No One Will Save You,” a nearly dialogue-free alien invasion movie.

Beyond their high concepts, Duffield’s works are marked by an emotional heft, which is no different in “Whalefall.” Jay’s diving trip is prompted by him trying to locate the body of his estranged father Mitt (Josh Brolin) after he dies by suicide. He’d never be able make amends with, or come to an understanding with his father, a theme that resonates through much of the story.

“I don’t think I was looking for a father-son story, but I think I needed a father-son story,” Duffield, a parent himself, says. “As soon as I was reading it, I couldn’t stop thinking about … not the whale, but about Jay and Mitt in that relationship. I thought, ‘That was the magic trick of the book.’ You’re forgetting about squids and acid and you’re thinking more about how these two guys are thinking they want nothing more than to spend time together, but they can’t quite express how they need to spend time in a different way.”

While Abrams and Brolin were able to bring the emotional gravitas to flashback scenes chronicling key moments in their frayed relationship, shooting the in-whale scenes was the overarching creative challenge.

“I had plenty of directors come and visit and all of them just looked so baffled,” Duffield says. “I had general confusion about how we were doing what we were doing. The thing I’ve learned the most is the joy of making movies for me is the crew and getting to hire a lot of the same people over and over again. I think if I have any gift as a director, it’s hiring people that are extremely talented, Oscar winners and whatnot. I like spending time with them and feel comfortable asking advice. I trust them if I feel like they have a note or an idea — it’s probably good.”

It’s part of a larger ethos Duffield brings to every project.

“I want to feel the effort, and I want to feel like I’m becoming a better filmmaker because of it,” he says.

article_text:
Dayanita Singh at ARCHIVIO , Archivio di Stato, Venice, 2026 Photograph by Mark Henley

Interviews - October 9, 2026

Earlier this year, the artist Dayanita Singh staged an unusual exhibition in Venice. She wanted to present a project during the Venice Biennale but to avoid the enormous financial and practical costs associated with the world’s most famous art extravaganza. Singh, who has photographed archives in Italy for more than a decade—and whose own voluminous archive has been the subject of many inventive installations—worked with the national archives at the Archivio di Stato, which provided an airy, double-height storage room (otherwise closed to the public) where shelves were lined with boxes of official documents. Singh’s own black-and-white photographs were arranged on fifteen four-sided, freestanding (but collapsible) wooden structures, inviting visitors into a choreographic experience arranged with minimal shipping expenses. Students served as docents in exchange for Singh’s mentorship, part of what she calls the “friendship economy” she relied upon to produce ARCHIVIO . In June, I visited the space with Singh, who told me why she considerers herself an archivist and how photography can democratize the art world.

ARCHIVIO , Archivio di Stato, Venice, 2026. All photographs by Luca Girardini

Sarah Meister: How did your ARCHIVIO exhibition come about? And how did you learn about the Archivio di Stato?

Dayanita Singh: In 2002, I was an artist in residence at the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum in Boston. And I was photographing chairs, because at the Gardner Museum, what can you do, right? So that’s where my chair obsession started. And then, Pieranna Cavalchini, the curator of contemporary art, said, “If you’re going to focus on chairs, you have to photograph some Renaissance chairs.”

So, she brought me to Florence, to Fausto Calderai, who’s a furniture historian, who also introduced me to chairs, but he also introduced me to his friend who looked after the Corsini Archive. When I went to the Corsini Archive, my jaw dropped. A little bit like when I first went to the Vespa factory in India.

Meister: That’s an amazing archive.

Singh: But then, as you know, I did a lot of work with archives in India. Later, around 2013 and 2014, Pieranna introduced me to Barbara Bianchini and Luigi Vigevani, who have an apartment in Venice. They’re professors in Milan, and they offered to let me to stay there. I walk into the apartment, and they had acquired work from my Hamburger Bahnhof show in 2003. So they said, “Stay.” [ laughs ]

I had been in the Venice Biennale in 2011 and in 2013, so I was familiar with Venice. My friend Massimo Warglien, a professor at Ca’ Foscari University, said that they’re doing a project with Archivio Stato with IBM. He thought it would be interesting for me to see this archive. So, it was because of Massimo that I got permission to come to the archive. This was maybe 2015. And from then on, every time I could come to Venice, I came because of this archive.

I’ve been photographing in this room for ten years, and then the director of the archive invites me to do a show here, about a year and a half ago. And I said, “Of course. It’s a dream. I would love to.”

Meister: One of the things that I think you and I both love about photography is how it helps us catalog and understand the world around us. I just saw the Spanish Pavilion, where Oriol Vilanova installed thousands of postcards. The space where you have been working is a space where the impulse to catalog is functioning almost on a municipal level. How do photographs and memories move from that institutional idea into something else for you?

Singh: You know what it’s made me realize is that for all the things I’m not—I’m not a photographer, I’m not this, I’m not that. I am an archivist. And I think that’s what I’ve done my whole life, is to archive places, people that I’ve been drawn to. So, of course, it’s a completely subjective archive. It was impossible to make these pillars just with images of the archives, so instead I started to excavate my own archive of twenty-five years.

Meister: All in Italy.

Singh: Yeah, all in Italy. Because, because of this friendship network that got set up.

Meister: These institutional archives are organized according to a certain municipal function. But the archives in your own home are different. How do you approach that? Because I’ve seen you sort and re-sort and re-sort.

Singh: So, the archive keeps shifting, much to the annoyance of anyone who might want to look through it. These were cataloged as chairs, and there’s a chairs folder. For ARCHIVIO , we have cities—Palermo, Naples—and that made it the most direct connection to this show. But I’m not sure. I mean, here is Rome. Other than say the Colosseum there, you don’t see Rome. You don’t see Palermo. And yet friends from Rome tell me this is more Rome than any big image of Rome. So, I went from my cataloging things like glass or statues to places. The other thing was to try and think of the form.

Meister: I do feel for whoever is responsible for your archive eventually, because they’re bound to wonder, “Was she thinking about stone? Was she thinking about place?”

Singh: Yeah. But every time I look at my archive, it changes, you know?

Meister: Andrea Anastasio described your work as a “relational cartography,” which I thought just beautifully captured the idea of the human centeredness but also the expansiveness. It’s a cartography of the world. What do you think of that idea?

Singh: I loved that he saw it was a human cartography—such a lovely word.

Meister: One of the interesting things around archives I think is the question of access. I’m curious how you approach that in your work?

Singh: For one, it was to make this space accessible so that people who live in the neighborhood, you know, it’s the first time those doors have been opened to the public.

For me, art is dissemination. So, when I call myself an offset artist, it’s not just the printing. It’s the dissemination.

Meister: And when they pulled them open, it was monumental.

Singh: Exactly. One of the main intentions of ARCHIVIO was to make the archive accessible in some form. People can’t go everywhere else, but at least they can see one cloister, and the room. And the work doesn’t even feel like an exhibition, because to me, it feels like it just grew out of the floor.

An interesting thing comes up in talking to the director of the archive and archivists. See, when I go to an archive, I don’t really open up anything. I don’t ask them. The archivist said, “You’ve never asked me to look at any document.” It’s the way archivists work, because in a lifetime you might only go through one shelf.

But you have to be able to read the code of the archive. And I thought that’s so much like my photography, where I have a certain map with which I enter a place. So, if I was coming to see you in Texas, I would first find out if there was a house museum there because that tells me something about a place. You know, people go to markets, people go to museums. This idea of the archivist photographer has become quite an important thought for me.

Meister: I think preservation is such an interesting thing. And there are different ways of thinking about preservation. I remember so fondly when you were at MoMA and all you wanted was for people to be able to touch your work.

Singh: Yeah.

Meister: I’d love to hear you speak about how you navigated the question of preservation here, from touching to organizing to temperature.

Singh: What I did here was I made exhibition copies. Because one of the things I don’t like about photography is that it’s so sensitive. That it has to be dark. You couldn’t be showing in a museum, you couldn’t have this kind of light for four months. And so I made exhibition copies.

Meister: I chuckled when I read Aruna D’Souza’s review in The New York Times , where she wrote, “What if I told you the most compelling art show in Venice right now consisted of black-and-white photos of Italian archives?” I love that what seems so incredible to the art world of course feels very natural.

Singh: Yes.

Meister: Would you talk about a few of the ways in which ARCHIVIO was so different from any other kind of installation in Venice now?

Singh: Well, mainly there was no sponsor. And I analyzed the costs involved in Venice. It would be about 150,000 euros, not for making the work, but just for various things. And each of those became a challenge for me. If I wanted docents for six months, 25,000 euros. Instead, we made a collaboration with Ca’ Foscari, and the Italian Cultural Institute in Delhi covered the shipping. I have docents here from Ca’ Foscari and Iuav University of Venice. They get credit. I mentor them.

Then I was told that lighting here would be 10,000 euros to light a show like this. And I said, “I’m perfectly happy with it.” But they said, “It’ll become dark early.” So, I said, “We’ll close the show early. We don’t have to have it till November. I’m not connected to this biennale.” And in fact, I didn’t open with the biennale. I opened with the literature festival to make that point. And that is the strength of photography, that it can go into so many different areas, no?

Meister: I agree. I’d be interested to hear you just share a little bit about where you see the democracy of photography, where you see its frailty, its edges, its constraints. Both how they’re operating here and about a way they might function, let’s say, in a space like Aperture in New York.

Singh: I think, I think going forward, it’s going to be the wall book for me. A wall book is that delicious space between being a print on the wall and a book in your bookshelf. I want to make a book that can be displayed on the wall as you would a watercolor, but still remain true to the book.

Meister: Are they different sizes?

Singh: No. It’s all the same size. They have sixty images and sixty different covers. And that’s all that would be available at one time. So, if you want this one, you have to get there in time.

Meister: Because otherwise there are only fifty-nine images left.

Singh: Yeah. Otherwise, you can get this one.

Meister: The work is the book. The covers are what vary and they reflect each of the pages of what’s inside. But the interiors of the books are the same.

Singh: Exactly. Like the Museum of Chance .

Meister: Everyone ultimately has access to the same thing.

Singh: And photography can really democratize the art world. But instead, we’ve gone the same route, right? With larger, larger prints, smaller, smaller editions—I’m part of that world—and higher prices. I think with the book object, everybody will find their own forms for it. I come from photography. For me, art is dissemination. So, when I call myself an offset artist, it’s not just the printing. It’s the dissemination.

ARCHIVIO was presented at the Archivio di Stato, Venice, from April 17–July 31, 2026, and is on view at the Museo Nazionale Etrusco di Villa Giulia, Rome, through January 3, 2027.

article_text:
Jon Stewart isn’t giving up his “Daily Show” chair just yet.

The comedian has extended his deal to host the Comedy Central talk show on Monday nights through 2028, with a rotating cast of correspondents including Ronny Chieng, Josh Johnson, Jordan Klepper, Michael Kosta, and Desi Lydic continuing to handle hosting duties Tuesday through Thursday. The move will keep Stewart on the air through two more election cycles, with his tenure notably scheduled to end at the same time as Donald Trump’s second presidential term.

The announcement comes amid Paramount absorbing Warner Bros. Discovery and becoming Skydance, and how the newly formed conglomerate will handle provocative late night hosts has been a hot topic, given controversies over Stephen Colbert’s exit from the airwaves and the overhaul of “60 Minutes.” But for now, one of the company’s most politically outspoken voices remains untouched. Questions remain for former “Daily Show” correspondent John Oliver and his HBO series “Last Week Tonight,” which is now owned by Skydance.

“Jon Stewart is a generational talent and The Daily Show continues to be one of the most influential franchises on television and a cornerstone of Comedy Central. We are excited to continue our partnership with Jon and his award winning news team,” George Cheeks, co-chair and chief content officer of Skydance TV , said in a statement.

Stewart famously hosted “The Daily Show” from 1999 through February 2015. His coverage of the Bush and Obama administrations on the show made him arguably the definitive political comedian of the early 21st century. After leaving the show, he remained active as a political commentator, directing the 2020 campaign finance satire “Irresistible” and hosting the short-lived Apple TV series “The Problem with Jon Stewart.”

After a nine-year hiatus, Stewart returned to “The Daily Show” in 2024, agreeing to host the show on Monday nights through that year’s presidential election. He has continued in that capacity for two additional years, and the new deal ensures that his second stint with the show will last for at least five years.

In addition to hosting once a week, Stewart will continue to serve as an executive producer on “The Daily Show” alongside showrunner Jen Flanz and his longtime manager James Dixon. He also hosts “The Weekly Show” podcast in addition to his on-air hosting duties.

editorial_title_zh: 从被拍摄的身体到其声音的消解：罗马 MACRO 博物馆秋季展核心的凝视
editorial_excerpt_zh: 在罗马的 MACRO 博物馆，玛丽阿尔巴·鲁索（Marialba Russo）的摄影作品对规范化的身体凝视提出了质疑，而两件声音作品则通过声音以及一座化为内心风景的城市的痕迹，唤起了莫妮卡·维蒂（Monica Vitti）的存在。本文将探讨…
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "“根据目前终于受到质疑、但绝未被彻底超越的习俗与惯例，男性行动，女性出场。男性看着女性。女性看着自己被看，”约翰·伯格（John Berger）在20世纪70年代初其基于同名 BBC 节目的知名著作《观看之道》（Ways of Seeing）开篇时指出，这是最早对视觉文化批评产生影响的文本之一，探讨了艺术与媒体中特定的具代表性惯例如何助长对现实的特定理解。几年后，电影评论家劳拉·穆尔维（Laura Mulvey）在其论文《视觉快乐与叙事电影》（Visual Pleasure and Narrative Cinema）中，将“男性凝视”（male gaze）这一概念进行理论化并使其普及，即大众传媒中构建女性形象时所采用的特权化和异性恋规范的视角。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/01_Marialba-Russo-Travestimento_1975-80-3-698x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Marialba Russo, Travestimento, 1975", "credit": "Exibart", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "正是在艺术领域开始对性别认同相关刻板印象提出质疑的大致同期，玛丽阿尔巴·鲁索在罗马 MACRO 博物馆汇集的七组摄影研究也诞生了。“反向凝视”（Sguardo rovescio，由克里斯蒂安娜·佩雷拉与埃琳娜·马吉尼策展，展期至2027年1月31日）这一标题已经暗示了对传统规范凝视的颠覆，其特别聚焦于对男子气概及其阴暗面的呈现。鲁索将节日和仪式选作优选的观察场所，捕捉并定格了脆弱解放的瞬间：在这些瞬间中，通过即兴舞蹈、换装和共同的仪式，社会上本不可动摇的身份与角色得以暂时改变形态。例如《在餐厅，1974年9月29日》（Al ristorante, il 29 settembre 1974，1974年）便记录了两位来自蒙特韦代圣母朝圣地（Santuario della Madonna di Monteverde）的年轻男子进行秘密舞蹈的序列。而在狂欢节期间描绘男性字面意义上穿上他人衣物的系列作品《换装》（Travestimento，1975–80）和《分娩》（Il Parto，1978）中，这种颠覆则更为明确。", "links": [{"text": "MACRO di Roma", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/mostre/da-hito-steyerl-alla-mostra-sul-premio-strega-cosa-vedere-nella-nuova-stagione-del-macro-di-roma/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/Marialba-Russo.-Sguardo-rovescio-installation-view-Roma-2026.-Photo-OKNO-studio.-Courtesy-MACRO-–-Museo-d’Arte-Contemporanea-di-Roma-6a-1024x682.jpg", "alt": "marialba russo", "caption": "Marialba Russo. Photo OKNO studio. Courtesy MACRO – Museo d’Arte Contemporanea di Roma", "credit": "Exibart", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "维蒂隐秘地回到了 Scanner 创作于2002年的作品《52个空间》（52 Spaces）中，该作品灵感源自米开朗基罗·安东尼奥尼（Michelangelo Antonioni）的《奇遇》（L’eclisse）。在此，身体彻底消解，留下的只有声音、噪声、音乐，以及通过当代罗马的录音被解构又重组的一部电影的氛围。安东尼奥尼的城市由此化为一片内心风景，电影与城市肌理在其中通过声音被剥离至最简。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
«Secondo l’uso e le convenzioni che sono finalmente in discussione, ma non sono state in alcun modo superate, gli uomini agiscono e le donne appaiono. Gli uomini guardano le donne. Le donne si guardano guardando» osserva John Berger all’inizio degli anni ‘70 nel noto libro Ways of Seeing basato sull’omonima serie BBC, fra i primi testi di critica della cultura visiva a mettere in discussione come determinate convenzioni rappresentative nell’arte e nei media favoriscano particolari comprensioni della realtà. Pochi anni dopo, sarà la critica cinematografica Laura Mulvey con il saggio Visual Pleasure and Narrative Cinema a teorizzare e rendere popolare il concetto di male gaze, ovvero il punto di vista privilegiato ed eteronormativo attraverso cui la figura femminile viene costruita nei mezzi di comunicazione di massa.

All’incirca negli stessi anni in cui, nel campo delle arti, iniziavano a essere messi in discussione gli stereotipi legati all’identità di genere, risalgono anche i sette nuclei della ricerca fotografica di Marialba Russo riuniti al MACRO di Roma . Sguardo rovescio – a cura di Cristiana Perrella ed Elena Magini , visitabile fino al 31 gennaio 2027 – allude già nel titolo al ribaltamento di uno sguardo tradizionalmente normativo, concentrandosi in particolare sulla rappresentazione della mascolinità e le sue zone d’ombra. Adottando la festa e il rito a luoghi privilegiati di osservazione, Russo intercetta e cattura momenti di fragile liberazione in cui attraverso balli improvvisati, travestimenti e ritualità condivise le identità e i ruoli socialmente immutabili possono temporaneamente cambiare forma. È questo il caso di Al ristorante, il 29 settembre 1974 (1974), una sequenza che registra il ballo clandestino di due giovani uomini provenienti dal Santuario della Madonna di Monteverde. Più esplicito è il rovesciamento che avviene nella serie Travestimento (1975–80) e ne Il Parto (1978), in cui in occasione di feste carnevalesche vengono ritratti uomini letteralmente in vesti altrui.

È invece attraverso il rito che Il Passaggio – l’incanata (1979) e L’espulsione del male (1974) portano il corpo al centro della scena; nei gesti di antichi rituali di iniziazione e guarigione, Russo documenta uno spazio in cui paure collettive, credenze e desideri di trasformazione trovano una forma visibile.

Alla ricerca antropologica e sociale – a cui è dedicata la mostra parallela Immagini della Madonna dell’Arco (After) a cura di Cristiana Perrella , Elena Magini , Andrea Viliani e Francesca Romana Uccella in mostra fino al 20 novembre 2026 al MUCIV–Museo delle Civiltà – fanno da contrappeso un paio di progetti caratterizzati da quello sguardo apparentemente distaccato e oggettivo tipico della fotografia in questi anni. Della serie delle centotrenta figure di spalle (1981) e Cult Fiction (1978-80) sono due progetti che mettono sapientemente di fronte, o meglio di spalle, un ritratto collettivo e codificato della mascolinità con la rappresentazione del desiderio sessuale che ne deriva, in un dialogo silenzioso in cui la serialità e la falsa neutralità del dispositivo fotografico finiscono per rivelare la posizione di chi guarda e soprattutto, di chi viene guardata.

Dalla presenza fisica dei corpi nelle fotografie di Russo il percorso del MACRO si sposta sulle tracce che sopravvivono attraverso rielaborazioni altrui. Nella Sala Video e Audio fino all’8 novembre, Maria’s Dream di Gaia De Megni e 52 Spaces di Robin Rimbaud aka Scanner a cura di Maria Lodovica Ferrari , due lavori in cui aleggia la presenza di Monica Vitti. In Maria’s Dream De Megni percorre la ricerca ossessiva e inquieta dalla tomba dell’antidiva al cimitero monumentale del Verano di Roma, sullo sfondo di un dialogo familiare dal sapore di casa in cui riflessioni sulla rappresentazione della donna e del ruolo femminile si intrecciano a racconti di vita quotidiana e ricordi scambiati fra madre e figlia.

Clandestinamente, Vitti ritorna in 52 Spaces , lavoro del 2002 di Scanner ispirato a L’eclisse di Michelangelo Antonioni. Qui il corpo è completamente dissolto, ne rimangono le voci, i rumori, la musica, le atmosfere di un film scomposto e ricomposto attraverso registrazioni della Roma contemporanea. La città di Antonioni diventa così un paesaggio interiore nel quale il cinema e il tessuto urbano vengono ridotti all’osso attraverso i suoni.

article_text:
2027年11月に東京・浜松町駅前に開館予定の「港区立みなと芸術センター m〜m（むーむ）」が、「開館1年前 プロローグ・イベント」を11月28日に開催する。アートや古典芸能、街歩きなどを通して、施設の目指す姿をひと足先に体験できる。

港区の文化芸術の中核拠点となる「m〜m」は、舞台芸術やアートなどを鑑賞するだけでなく、人々が自ら表現や創造に取り組む機会も提供する施設。子供から大人まで、様々な背景を持つ人々が交流し、新たな発見やつながりを生み出すことを目指す。今回のイベントでは、アーティストや文化人によるプログラムを通して、芸術と地域、人と人とが交わる可能性を紹介する。

注目のひとつが、アーティスト・コレクティブ SIDE CORE によるウォーキングツアー「Looking from inside outside」だ。浜松町駅周辺から港区の湾岸地域を歩き、街に残る歴史の痕跡や、変化し続ける都市の姿を探る。ストリートカルチャーを切り口に、公共空間や都市における表現の可能性を考えてきたSIDE COREの視点を通して、普段見慣れた街の別の一面に出会う機会となりそうだ。

また、木ノ下歌舞伎を主宰する 木ノ下裕一 と、慶應義塾大学教授の 都倉武之 による特別対談「物語の生まれる場所へ〜港区編」も開催。古典芸能と土地の関係を探ってきた木ノ下と、港区の歴史研究に携わる都倉が、地域にどのような物語が生まれ、受け継がれてきたのかを語り合う。

このほか、音声や文字、手話など、異なる「ことば」を手がかりに物語をつくる、 めとてラボ のワークショップ「ことばのあいだで、物語をつくろう！」も実施。ろう者と聴者、子供と大人など、参加者がそれぞれの表現を持ち寄り、思いがけない解釈や物語が生まれる過程を楽しむ。会場では、開館予定の施設をVRで体験できる「バーチャルm〜m Version 2.0」や、砂浜をイメージした自由に過ごせるスペース、ヴァイオリニストの 石上真由子 とチェリストの 水野優也 によるミニコンサートも予定している。

メインホールでは、映画監督の 深田晃司 や俳優・日本舞踊家の 藤間爽子 らゲストと、港区長の 清家愛 が登壇するトークセッションも実施。お笑い芸人の 濱田祐太郎 による漫談のほか、 桂福壱 による手話落語、 三遊亭遊雀 による港区にゆかりのある古典落語も披露される。手話通訳や字幕を取り入れ、異なる言語や聴覚の在り方を持つ人々がともに楽しめるプログラムとなっている。

「開館1年前 プロローグ・イベント」は、11月28日11時から18時まで、浜松町コンベンションホールにて開催。入場は無料だが、プログラムによって事前予約が必要なものや、参加人数に制限があるものもある。各プログラムの詳細や参加方法は 公式サイト で確認できる。

article_text:
Darren Aronofsky will receive the Award for Director at the 34th Toruń Camerimage International Film Festival in Poland.

The festival, which celebrates the art of cinematography, will take place Nov. 7-14 in Toruń, Poland. Organizers announced the honor Thursday, recognizing the Oscar-winning director’s distinctive approach to filmmaking and his longstanding collaborations with cinematographers, particularly Matthew Libatique, who has shot much of the director’s work.

Related Stories

Omar Sy on Taking Creative Control of Netflix's 'Lupin' and Why 'Black Dumas' Will Spark Political Debate in France

“Honouring Aronofsky at ToruńCamerimage is a tribute to a director whose work demonstrates the immense power of cinema when form becomes an integral part of the story being told,” festival organizers said in a statement.

Aronofsky made his feature directorial debut with the psychological thriller “Pi” in 1998, which earned him the directing award at Sundance. He followed it with 2000’s “Requiem for a Dream,” starring Jared Leto, Jennifer Connelly, Marlon Wayans and Ellen Burstyn, who received an Oscar nomination for her performance.

His 2008 drama “The Wrestler,” starring Mickey Rourke, won the Golden Lion at the Venice Film Festival, while 2010’s “Black Swan,” starring Natalie Portman, earned five Academy Award nominations, including best picture and best director. Portman won the Oscar for best actress for her performance.

Aronofsky’s other directing credits include “The Fountain,” “Noah” and “mother!” His 2022 drama “The Whale” marked Brendan Fraser’s return to a leading film role and earned the actor his first Academy Award. Most recently, Aronofsky directed the 2025 crime thriller “Caught Stealing,” starring Austin Butler, Zoë Kravitz and Regina King.

Camerimage, one of the world’s leading festivals dedicated to cinematography, annually recognizes filmmakers and cinematographers for their contributions to visual storytelling. Its main competition awards the Golden Frog for outstanding cinematography, alongside a series of honorary awards recognizing achievements across the filmmaking industry.

New Classics Pictures’ crime procedural drama “ Traces of Justice ” rebounded to first place at the mainland China box office during the Nov. 6–8 weekend, collecting RMB21.5 million ($3.2 million) over the three-day frame, according to data from Artisan Gateway.

The performance lifted the multi-decade investigation epic to $103.7 million since its Oct. 1 release. Directed by Chen Sicheng (“Detective Chinatown”) and co-written with Zhang Ji and Yan Zijie, the drama stars Zhang Yi, Ma Li, and Chen Minghao alongside Karry Wang, Fan Chengcheng, and Chen Feiyu in a narrative tracking an elite public security detective solving complex historical cases based on real events.

Constantin Film and Sony Pictures’ horror reboot “ Resident Evil ” moved to second position after a month-long reign atop the charts, taking in $3 million in its fifth weekend. The video game adaptation has now reached a cumulative haul of $76 million since launching during the Golden Week corridor on Oct. 5.

Tencent Penguin Pictures’ road drama “ Embers ” debuted in third place, grossing $2.1 million across its two-day opening frame following a Saturday, November 7 rollout. Written and directed by Sun Aoqian, the film stars Song Jia as a weary crematorium worker who accidentally mixes up two sets of funeral ashes. When the families refuse to switch them back, she partners with the deceased’s daughter, played by Vicky Chen, on a journey across the country to return the remains. The cast also features Zu Feng.

Shanghai Captain’s rural black comedy-thriller “ The Coffin Swap ” opened in fourth position, pulling in $1.7 million over its two-day weekend debut. Directed by He Nian from a script by Chen Lu, the feature re-adapts Xin Yukun’s 2014 mystery classic “Deep in the Heart” through the lens of He’s acclaimed stage production. Starring Jiang Wu, Du Guangyi, Gu Xin, Fan Yilin, and Wang Weishuai, the narrative unfolds in a secluded village thrown into chaotic intrigue and conflicting cover-ups after an unidentified charred body is discovered.

Beijing Joy Fun Pictures’ body-swap comedy “Mr. & Mrs. Pardon” rounded out the top five, adding $1.4 million in its sixth weekend to lift its cumulative gross to $61.3 million. Directed by Shen Chunyang and written by Ma Duo, the satirical feature stars real-life comedic pair Shen Chunyang and Xiao Shenyang alongside Jia Bing and Yu Yang as an uninspired middle-aged couple forced to navigate marital strain after swapping bodies.

Mainland China’s overall weekend box office contracted to $16.4 million amid an ongoing fall lull. The 2026 year-to-date box office reached $4.75 billion, trailing the same period in 2025 by 29%.

article_text:
NYC Weekend Watch is our weekly round-up of repertory offerings.

BAM A Dean Stockwell retrospective features films by David Lynch , Joseph Losey , Jonathan Demme , plus Dennis Hopper’s Backtrack on 35mm; Playback offers films by Spike Lee and Gillo Pontecorvo ; Ken Russell’s reconstructed The Devils continues—read (or listen to) our interview with Mark Kermode on it.

Museum of the Moving Image James Gray’s New York features a print of Raging Bull ; a Kubrick series continues with A Clockwork Orange and The Killing on 35mm; Lynne Littman’s Testament shows on 35mm this Saturday.

Roxy Cinema Bill Gunn’s Personal Problems shows on Saturday, while Tickled plays Friday and Sunday.

Museum of Modern Art A Sergei Loznitsa retrospective continues while Sundays with Steven brings The Spy Who Came In from the Cold and Bridge of Spies .

Film Forum A 4K restoration of Zhang Yimou’s Raise the Red Lantern begins playing; The Red Balloon shows on Sunday.

Anthology Film Archives A German Punk series begins.

IFC Center Ken Russell’s reconstructed The Devils continues on a restored 35mm print—read (or listen to) our interview with Mark Kermode on it—while The Exorcist , The Holy Mountain , and Ju-On: The Grudge play late.

Nitehawk Prospect Park A print of JFK screens early on Saturday and Sunday.

Metrograph Bram Stoker’s Dracula , Sad Vacation , and Far from Heaven show on 35mm; Neuro-Noir , Kogonoda: A Way of Looking , and All Happy Families Are Alike start while Terence Fisher , The Leaves are Falling , Trains: Local Routes , and Winona Ryder continue.

On today’s episode of Variety ‘s “ Strictly Business ” podcast, movie marketing veteran Gerry Rich details his new memoir “Chasing Hollywood: A Marketing Chief’s Lessons on Breaking Through.”

Rich has worked for most of Hollywood’s major studios, including Paramount, Columbia Pictures, MGM, Miramax and Amazon MGM Studios. He looks back at moments of triumph such as the 2008 opening of “Iron Man,” which launched the Marvel Cinematic Universe. And Rich looks ahead to how the discipline of entertainment marketing and audience targeting is changing in the age of AI.

Related Stories

Pedro Pascal on Learning Cello for ‘Behemoth!,’ Why ‘You’ve Got to Eat S---’ to Make It in Hollywood and the ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Line His Character Says

'The Odyssey' Oscar Blitz to Begin With Robert Downey Jr., Guillermo del Toro and Steven Spielberg as Moderators

“Going back even a decade or two we had the ability to reach a broad audience all at one time. Through linear television and cable and sports and digital and social media, we were able to hit a broad swath of the audience in real time,” Rich says. “It’s much more difficult to do that now, particularly with linear TV. The only thing that really gets a significant audience is would be live sports, particularly football. That’s where we’re assured of getting a captive audience, a broad audience, a significant audience all at once. All of that has changed quite a bit.”

Rich recalls the heady experience of building buzz for the “Iron Man” release in 2008, when the industry was skeptical about the market for elevated superhero movie. And star Robert Downey Jr. had a lot to prove after public battles with personal demons that inevitably hurt his star power.

“ Iron Man didn’t have the notoriety as IP as Spider-Man or X-Men or any of the better known characters. So there was some uncertainty as to whether or not Iron Man would be able to resonate for the broadest audience and deliver superhero-type grosses. There was also a lot of skepticism about whether Robert Downey Jr. was the right guy to play this character, this flawed character. And there was a lot of questions as to whether or not [director] Jon Favreau could deliver a movie with the adequate and necessary scope and scale,” Rich recalls.

“But we really felt and as soon as we saw dailies that there was something really extraordinary happening with that movie. And what we decided to do was hold off showing any assets from the film until Comic-Con of 2007, well before the release of the movie,” he says. “And that’s when we brought the entire crew down [to Comic-Con]. Jon Favreau came out to a thunderous applause. And he had his iPhone, capturing the response of the audience and he just had the group from the very beginning. We showed the teaser trailer that we were going to launch, as well as some film footage, and the audience was sold. They came out as major champions of the film.”

article_text:
LuckyChap International, the London-based joint venture between LuckyChap and Mediawan that was unveiled in late 2025, has given its filmmaking ambitions a shot in the arm with a significant new hire.

Katie Goodson-Thomas , a hugely respected and experienced exec who has spent more than a decade at Searchlight Pictures , is set to leave the studio to join the LuckyChap International team in the new role of president of film.

Related Stories

Kevin Delaney Takes Role as NBC News' Head of Digital Content and Subscription

Working in close partnership with co-managing directors Mona Qureshi and Tanya Qureshi, who joined earlier this year, Goodson-Thomas will spearhead the film slate, with the LuckyChap International leadership trio working in collaboration with LuckyChap partners Margot Robbie, Tom Ackerley, Josey McNamara and Milan Popelka, alongside the broader U.S. team.

At Searchlight, where she was most recently executive vice president, co-head of production and development, Goodson-Thomas played a key role in expanding the studio’s U.K. presence, overseeing numerous award-winning films such as Yorgos Lanthimos’ “The Favourite” and “Poor Things,” Martin McDonagh’s “Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri,” “The Banshees of Inisherin” and the upcoming “Wild Horse Nine,” as well as “All of Us Strangers,” “The Roses” and Alice Birch’s forthcoming directorial debut “Sweetsick,” starring Cate Blanchett.

“We’re thrilled to welcome Katie to LuckyChap International,” said Mona Qureshi and Tanya Qureshi. “Her career embodies the kind of independent spirit and big-heartedness that inspires us, and her ambition, taste and creative instinct make her a natural fit for what we are building. We can’t wait to have her alongside us as a fellow journeywoman!”

Added Goodson-Thomas: “The LuckyChap team has exceptional taste, fearlessness and a creative identity entirely its own, as well as an infectious sense of possibility about what the company can achieve. Searchlight has been such an incredible creative home for me that I always knew it would take somewhere truly special to tempt me away. The opportunity to join that alongside Mona, Tanya and such a brilliant team was simply too exciting to resist. The U.K. and Europe are full of remarkable talent, and I’m hugely ambitious about what we can find, back and get made together.”

Goodson-Thomas will officially join LuckyChap International in the new year.

“We’re in awe of everything Katie has accomplished throughout her career, and we all feel extraordinarily privileged that she is bringing her undeniable creative talents, vision and depth of experience to LuckyChap International,” said LuckyChap’s US partners Robbie, Ackerley, McNamara and Popelka. “She’s such a kindred spirit culturally, and we’ve long admired her ability to spot exceptional filmmaking talent and champion their projects from the very beginning all the way through. We genuinely couldn’t be more excited to have her join us on this adventure, and to forge a killer slate together that we can all be incredibly proud of!”

Added Searchlight president Matthew Greenfield: “Katie has been a wonderful colleague all of these years and LuckyChap International is getting an exceptional and passionate advocate for filmmakers. We couldn’t be happier for her as she takes on this next chapter, and we’re excited to see all that she and the team will accomplish together.”

article_text:
Sung Tieu zeigte Angela Merkel die Plattenbausiedlung an der Gehrenseestraße in Berlin, in der sie als Kind lebte. Sie diente der Künstlerin als Ausgangspunkt für ihren Beitrag zum deutschen Pavillon auf der diesjährigen Venedig-Biennale

Es sei eines der unerwarteten Geschenke des Lebens, diesem besonderen Menschen die Gehrenseestraße zu zeigen, schrieb Sung Tieu bei Instagram auf Englisch und postete dazu ein Bild.

In dem Gebäude in Berlin-Lichtenberg hatten früher vietnamesische Vertragsarbeiter gewohnt. Tieu zog mit ihrer Mutter in das Wohnheim und lebte dort mit ihr in einem Zimmer. "Bei der Recherche dazu wurde mir klar, dass meine Kindheit dort in engem zeitlichem Zusammenhang mit beispielsweise den Pogromen in Rostock-Lich­tenhagen stand", sagt die Künstlerin im Monopol-Interview . "Anfang der 1990er-Jahre unternahmen Rechtsextreme den Versuch, einen Pogrom gegen die Gehrenseestraße zu organisieren, der von Bürgerinnen und Bürgern in der Nachbarschaft aufgehalten wurde."

Für die diesjährige Biennale baute sie die Plattenbaufassade in Venedig nach . Sie verkleidete den deutschen Pavillon dafür mit rund drei Millionen Mosaiksteinen.

"Blick auf DDR-Geschichte sehr interessant"

Merkels Büro bestätigte den Besuch. Die frühere Kanzlerin finde den diesjährigen Beitrag Deutschlands zur Kunstbiennale in Venedig – den von Sung Tieu und der leider verstorbenen Henrike Naumann – "auch mit Blick auf die DDR-Geschichte sehr interessant", hieß es. Merkel wuchs selbst im Osten auf. Die CDU-Politikerin war von 2005 bis 2021 Bundeskanzlerin.

Im Berliner Bode-Museum wird derzeit auch ein Porträtgemälde von Merkel ausgestellt, das schon viel Publikum angezogen hat. Auf der diesjährigen Kunstbiennale in Venedig war Merkel nach Angaben ihres Büros nicht. Die Ausstellung läuft noch bis 22. November.
